232: The respondent was charged with various offences alleged to have been committed by him in the course of his raid as an armed gang on a certain factory known as the Jessop Factory at Dum Dum. He was convicted and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment by the Special Court constituted under section 5 (1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, but was acquitted by the High Court. On appeal by the State Government to this Court it was contended that the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure for trial of warrant cases by Magistrates was not reasonable and that the provisions of article 14 of the Constitution were violated inasmuch as the procedure laid down by the Code for trial of warrants case by Magistrates was unreasonable and discriminatory. Held, that the procedure laid 'down by the Code was not arbitrary nor did it offend against article 14 Of the Constitution. The classification made by the Legislature between those who were tried before a special court and those who were trying or sentencing by a special tribunal was not arbitrary and had no relation to any unreasonableness or fairness. The classification was based upon an intelligible differentia which distinguished those whose trial was by a special court from those who were being tried by a special Tribunal. The classification could not be regarded as arbitrary as there would have been some intelligible differentiation between those who are being tried by the special tribunal and those who are trying or sentencing. The classification must not be arbitrary but should be based upon an objective set out in the Act and that arbitrariness must be eliminated from the well recognised canon of construction by imposing a sentence which is just and fair having regard to the object and purpose of the Act.

It speaks of the authority empowered to remove from the service any person subject to the act. The Central Government has been given the power to dismiss or remove from the serv ice any person subject thereto. The Central Gove rnment can dismiss or remove a person from the service. 715: The appellant No. 1 was a bus conductor in the respondent company. On December 13, 1951, the Conciliation Officer wrote to the appellant No. I and enclosed the demands of the Union which were dated August 9, 1951. The appellants did not give any reply to the said demand but on March 18, 1952, the Chief Presidency Magistrate dismissed the appellants ' complaint under section 31(1) Of the , against them and the two appellants and the partners of the appellant No 1. The appellants filed an application before the High Court for quashing the aforesaid order of dismissal under section 31 Of the Act. The High Court held that as the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952, further proceedings for conciliation were illegal and therefore the accused persons could not be convicted under section 31 (1). Held, that the provisions of section 12(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, are mandatory and do not confer upon the accused persons any right to be tried by a court during the period of conciliation proceedings. Section 12(6), however, does not preclude the appropriate Government from making a reference to a Labour Court or a Tribunal during such period. The words " during the period" in section 12(4)(b) only mean " time during the pendency of any conciliation proceedings". The words " time during trial of any proceeding under this Act" in section 20(2)(b) of the Act means " time during investigation of the charges made" in section 23(a) of the . In the present case the conciliation proceedings were pending when the Act came into force and the report under section 12( 6 ) was submitted by the Conciliation Officer. The Act does not contemplate the submission of the report by the Conciliation officer within 24 hours of its receipt by the appropriate Government. The Act contemplates the submission of a report by the conciliation officer within 24 hrs. of the date of commencement of the conciliation proceedings. The Act is intended to provide a complete machinery for settlement of industrial disputes and it cannot be interpreted to mean that the conciliation proceedings should be treated as terminated when the report under s.12(6) is received by the appropriate government.
6245: The State Public Service Commission, in exercise of the power conferred by Rule 4(2) of the Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission (Limited Recruitment) Rules, 1975 invited applications from eligible candidates for recruitment to the post of Upper Zila Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women 's Branch). The written examination was conducted on May 5, 1985 and the viva voce test was held on June 8, 1985. On the basis of the results thereof the successful candidates were called to be interviewed. The interviews were held on July 14, 1986 and the result was declared on August 22, 1987. The selected candidates were asked to join their posts within a month thereafter. In the writ petitions filed before the High Court challenging the selection of the successful candidates on the ground that they had better performance in the written examination than those who had secured lesser marks in the written examina tion than them, it was contended that the entire process of recruit ment was vitiated as the interviews had been conducted in violation of the rules and that the entire selection was vitiated. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The process of recruitment is regulated by the statutory rules framed under Article 309 of the Constitution. These rules are framed under Article 77 of the Constitution which have the force of law. They do not provide for any consultation with the Public Service Commission. The procedure prescribed under the statutory rules has to be followed while conducting the recruitment. [864F] 1.2 The manner of conducting the recruitment has also been provided under Rule 9 of the Rules. It is only after the selection is over that the question of determining the suitability of the candidates would arise. [865G H; 866A] 1.3 The Commission is bound to hold the viva voce examination. The Commission has no discretion in the matter. The Government may prescribe the mode of such examination or conduct the viva voce. The method of conducting the viva voce is left to the Government. The word "income" has no wider meaning than the word 'profits and gains" in section 24B. It means income derived from property held under trust wholly for charitable purposes. 1778: The appellant was an employee of the respondent company. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging his dismissal from service and prayed for a direction to the company to reinstate him with full back wages. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The award made by the Industrial Tribunal could not be said to amount to a contract of employment within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. [864 C] (ii) The terms of the award did not fall within the definition prescribed by section 2(v) of the Industrial Disputes Act. It is now well settled that when an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law, the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structure prescribed by the award. Therefore, in substance, it must be shown that they constitute part of the terms of the contract of employment either express or implied. [865 D E; 866 A] (iii) The terms and conditions of service of the appellant were governed by the terms of his service and he had no right to remain in service until he attained the age of superannuation. The terms of his appointment were governed by Standing Orders which provided for the termination of service on reaching the age of Superannuation. The Standing Orders were not applicable to the appellant as he was not a workman. [867 B C]

6118: The petitioners are carpenters, 1st and 2nd grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of the Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation. In 1951, the testator died and after his death on September 26, 1945, respondent 1 filed a suit for declaration that the said will was not genuine and that he was entitled to dispose of the properties by a will. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed it and held that the will set up by the appellant was not genuine. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The question whether a will is genuine or not has to be determined with reference to the terms of the document itself. If the intention of the parties was that the property should remain vested in the legatee, then the intention could have been easily made by looking at the surrounding circumstances. [902 D E] (ii) It is well settled that if a will is found to be a registered one, it would be admissible in evidence under section 32(d) of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872, and the contents thereof would be proved as against all the persons whom it purports to be. But where the language used is clear and explicit and does not admit of any ambiguity, the surrounding circumstances may be taken into consideration. [903 G H; 904 A B] In the instant case, the will was not registered. The High Court was therefore right in holding that the will was genuine. [904 C]

1697: The appellant was a limited company carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of soaps. The Tribunal referred the question to the High Court for determination. 2207: The respondent was a dealer in goods. He purchased the business of one Purushottam Raju under the name All India Trading Company and carried on the same. 78: The appellant was the tenant of a flat in Bombay. He was charged under section 18(1) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, LVII of 1947 for receiving a sum or consideration as a condition of his tenancy. His defence was that he had been in possession of the flat for more than 12 years and that he had entered into negotiations with the complainant for a certain purpose. The complainant paid Rs. 29,500 to the appellant who was then in possession of a flat. The appellant was convicted by the Magistrate under section 19(2) of the Act and sentenced to one day 's simple imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 30,000. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one day simple imprisonment. The appellant contended that the word "relinquishment" in section 18(i) of the act must be construed in its widest sense and it should not be extended to the case of an assignment of tenancy. Held, that the word 'relinquishment ' is used in the wide sense of relinquishment of possession which implies an involuntary surrender of possession by the tenant. It does not include a relinquishment of something done in the exercise of the right of possession. The word "relin quire " means "to have the effect of relinquishing possession". The word "result" denotes an intention to relinquish. In the context of the Act there are two distinct concepts, namely, relinquishment of tenancy and compensation. The former is called a relinquishment and the latter is a payment or relinquishment. A relinquishment is the transfer of a thing or of another, and is called a surrender or charge. The relinquishment is for the benefit of the person paying or agreeing to pay the particular thing or thing; and the relinquishment is called a payment or a relinquishment. Where the term is used in contradistinction to the term of tenancy, the relinquishment may be express or implied, but where the term is not used in any strict sense, it cannot be said that the relinquishment involves relinquishment of property.

314: The appellant was put up for trial before the First Class Magistrate of Patiala, who committed him to stand his trial under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. 380: The appellants were displaced persons and the respondent entered into an agreement with them, under which they were put in possession of the mills and the factory on 31 8 1952. On January 11, 1956, the Trustees introduced another scheme for the working of the aforesaid two shift systems. Under this scheme, the shore crew at the Alexandi Dock were entitled to overtime of 8 hours per day. In 1957, the Trustees framed Rules under the Act, which provided that the employees should get overtime of 8 days in a week. Rule 4(1) provided that the rate of wages of all employees should be fixed on the basis of the total number of hours worked during a month. The appellants contended that the provisions of the Act were ultra vires the powers of the Trustees and that the rates of wages fixed by them were unreasonable and arbitrary. The Act did not provide for any fixation of hours of work or minimum wages but only made provision for the payment of remuneration in respect of such holidays and vacanci es. The Act also made provision for payment of extra wages to certain categories of employees. The Act was enacted with a view to ensure fair labour conditions among the workers employed in the establishment. It was not meant to make the employees work hours fixed according to the hours fixed. The Act does not provide for the fixing of hours of worlaness or minimum wages. The Act is not intended to confer higher benefits on the employees than are given to those employed in the establishments. The Act provides for the settlement of industrial disputes and the framing of rules for regulating their procedure. The Trustees have no power to fix the hours of work of any class of employees.

The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the termination of the appellant 's leasehold rights could only be done under the third proviso to section 10(1) and that the provisions of the Act were not applicable to the case. On appeal by special leave: Held, (i) that the words "foregoing proviso" in the first proviso to section 40(2)(b) of the Act refer to the third proviso, and not to the fourth proviso; (ii) that the effect of the second proviso is that the right created before the notified date but after July 1, 1945, for a period not exceeding one year would be valid and enforceable both by and against the Government by operation of the body of sub sections (1) and (2) of section 20 of the Act.
